## Chapter 1

CHAPTER XI: THE BATTLE OF THE RAMS (1863)

Minister Adams troubled himself little about what he did not see of an enemy. His son, a nervous animal, made life a terror by seeing too much. The Minister played his hand as it came, and seldom credited his opponents with greater intelligence than his own. Earl Russell suited him; perhaps a certain personal sympathy united them, and indeed Henry Adams never saw Russell without being amused by his droll likeness to John Quincy Adams. The Minister had nothing to lose by treating Russell as a friend, and whether Russell were true or false mattered less, because in either case the Legation could act only as though he were false.

Russell must have been greatly annoyed by Sir Robert Collier's hint of collusion with the rebel agents in the Alabama Case, but he hardened himself to hear the same innuendo repeated in nearly every note from the Legation. Whatever the theory, the action of diplomacy had to be the same. Minister Adams was obliged to imply collusion. He could not stop at criminal negligence: no one could be so simple as to believe that two armored ships-of-war could be built publicly, under the eyes of the Government, and go to sea like the Alabama, without active and incessant collusion.

As the spring of 1863 drew on, the vast field cleared itself for action. A campaign more beautiful — better suited for training the mind of a youth eager for training — has not often unrolled itself for study before a young man perched in so commanding a position. Very slowly, after two years of solitude, one began to feel the first faint flush of new and imperial life. One was twenty-five, and quite ready to assert it. At moments one's breath came quick. One began to dream the sensation of wielding unmeasured power. Little by little, behind the chaos in Washington, power was taking shape; massed and guided as it had not been before.

Life never could know more than a single such climax. As the huge masses struck, one after another, with the precision of machinery, the world shivered. During the July days Londoners were stupid with unbelief. They were learning from the Yankees how to fight.

News of Vicksburg and Gettysburg reached London one Sunday afternoon, and that evening Henry Adams went early to a small reception at Monckton Milnes's. He found only the ladies in the drawing-room. Presently the gentlemen came in, and, as luck would have it, Delane of the *Times* came first. When Milnes caught sight of his young American friend, with a whoop of triumph he rushed to throw both arms about his neck and kiss him on both cheeks. The private secretary had no thought of himself; he was thinking of Delane, whose eye caught his at the moment of Milnes's embrace. Delane probably regarded it as a piece of Milnes's foolery; the British mind is the slowest of all minds, and the capture of Vicksburg had not yet penetrated his thick cortex of fixed ideas.

Vicksburg and Gettysburg cleared the board. At the end of July, 1863, Minister Adams was ready to deal with Earl Russell or Lord Palmerston or Mr. Gladstone or Mr. Delane, or any one else who stood in his way.

In the Legation no great confidence was felt in stopping the rams. Russell seemed immovable. With loss of hope came the raising of tone, until at last, after stripping Russell of every rag of defence, the Minister closed with the famous sentence: "It would be superfluous in me to point out to your lordship that this is war!"

What the Minister meant was his own affair; what the private secretary understood was a part of his education. The fact had to be stated to make clear the issue. The war was Russell's war — Adams only accepted it. Russell's reply of September 8 announced at last that "instructions have been issued which will prevent the departure of the two ironclad vessels from Liverpool." The Legation accepted it as Grant had accepted the capitulation of Vicksburg. Though Minister Adams should stay in office till he were ninety, he would never fight another campaign of life and death like this. He felt respect for Russell as for Palmerston because they represented an English policy which, for four generations, every Adams had fought and exploited as the chief source of his political fortunes.

Again and again, in after life, Henry Adams went back over the ground to see whether he could detect error on either side. He found none. All the more he was disconcerted that Russell should indignantly, to his dying day, deny and resent the axiom of Adams's whole contention — that from the first he meant to break up the Union. Russell affirmed that he meant nothing of the sort; that he had meant nothing at all; that he meant to do right; that he did not know what he meant. Driven from one defence after another, he pleaded at last that he had no defence. What was worse for the private secretary — to the total derision and despair of the lifelong effort for education — he proved it.

The biography published in 1889 produced papers which upset all that Henry Adams had taken for diplomatic education. Russell proved that he had been feeble, timid, mistaken, senile, but not dishonest. The Lairds had built the ships in reliance on the law-officers' opinion that the statute did not apply. On September 3, two days before Mr. Adams's "superfluous" letter, Russell had already written to Palmerston in a state of belated alarm — calling "the conduct" of the rebel agents "suspicious" when no one else in Europe or America felt any suspicion about it — directing that the ships should be detained "as one of policy though not of strict law." He had simply neglected to notify the American Minister till the afternoon of September 5. The hilarity of the secretaries in Portland Place would have been loud had they seen the subsequent note to the Admiralty, suggesting they buy the ironclads from "Monsieur Bravay of Paris" — the Turkish Government having already been canvassed on the same errand.

These papers upset from top to bottom the results of the private secretary's diplomatic education forty years after he had supposed it complete. He found in the Life of Gladstone a remark several times repeated: "I always hold that politicians are the men whom, as a rule, it is most difficult to comprehend"; and Gladstone added: "For my own part, I never have thus understood, or thought I understood, above one or two."

Earl Russell was certainly not one of the two.

## Chapter 2

CHAPTER XII: ECCENTRICITY (1863)

Knowledge of human nature is the beginning and end of political education, but several years of arduous study near Westminster led Henry Adams to think that knowledge of English human nature had little or no value outside of England. The English mind was one-sided, eccentric, systematically unsystematic, and logically illogical. The less one knew of it, the better.

From the old-world point of view, the American had no mind; he had an economic thinking-machine which could work only on a fixed line. The American mind exasperated the European as a buzz-saw might exasperate a pine forest. The English mind disliked the French because it was antagonistic, perhaps hostile, but recognized it as at least a thought. The American mind was not a thought at all; it was a convention — superficial, narrow, ignorant — a mere cutting instrument, practical, economical, sharp, and direct.

The defect that most struck an American in the English was its enormous waste in eccentricity. Americans applied their whole energy with close economy; English society was eccentric by law and for sake of the eccentricity itself. The commonest phrase overheard at a London dinner-table was that So-and-So "is quite mad." Eccentricity was so general as to become hereditary distinction. It made the chief charm of English society as well as its chief terror. Society swarmed with exaggerated characters; it contained little else.

Often this eccentricity bore all the marks of strength; perhaps it was actual exuberance of force. The Bostonian called it national character — native vigor, robustness, courage — and respected and feared it. The private secretary began by regarding British eccentricity as a force. Contact with it, in the shape of Palmerston, Russell, and Gladstone, made him hesitate. Russell might be dishonest or merely obtuse; the English type might be brutal or only stupid; but strong, in either case, it was not, nor did it seem strong to Englishmen.

By natural affinity the social eccentrics commonly sympathized with political eccentricity. The English mind took naturally to rebellion — when foreign — and felt particular confidence in the Southern Confederacy because of its combined attributes: foreign rebellion of English blood. All the English eccentrics rushed into the ranks of rebel sympathizers, leaving few but well-balanced minds to attach themselves to the cause of the Union. The "cranks" were all rebels, and the list was portentous.

This eccentricity did not mean strength. The proof was the mismanagement of the rebel interests. In London society Mason counted merely as one eccentric more; he might have figured as a new Benjamin Franklin with all society at his feet, but Mr. Adams had his usual luck in enemies, who were always his most valuable allies if his friends only let them alone. Mason was his greatest diplomatic triumph. The Minister had his collision with Palmerston; he drove Russell off the field; he overbore Slidell; but he never lifted a finger against Mason, who became his bulwark of defence.

Never was there a moment when eccentricity, if it were a force, should have had more value to the rebel interest; and the managers must have thought so, for they accepted as their champion an eccentric of eccentrics. Mr. Roebuck had been a tribune of the people, and, like tribunes of most other peoples, in growing old, had grown fatuous. The Lairds let him represent them in his motion of June 30, 1863, to recognize the Confederacy; the private secretary, sent to the House to report, listened with great content while Bright caught and shook and tossed Roebuck as a big mastiff shakes a wiry, ill-conditioned, toothless, bad-tempered Yorkshire terrier. The result was not in doubt.

The question whether British eccentricity was ever strength weighed heavily in the balance of education. Bright's courage was almost as irrational as that of the rebels themselves. He struck, in succession, pretty nearly every man in England that could be reached by a blow, and when he could not reach the individual he struck the class. He could not act on the defensive; his mind required attack. Even at the dinner-table he talked as though denouncing his fellow-guests on a platform; his blow was elementary, like the thrash of a whale.

At a Trades-Union meeting at St. James's Hall in March 1863, Bright managed in his opening paragraph to insult or outrage every class of Englishman commonly considered respectable, and, for fear of any escaping, insulted them repeatedly under consecutive heads:—

"Privilege thinks it has a great interest in the American contest. It has beheld thirty million of men happy and prosperous, without emperors — without king — without nobles, except such as are made by eminence in intellect and virtue — without State bishops and State priests — without great armies and great navies — without a great debt and great taxes; and Privilege has shuddered at what might happen to old Europe if this great experiment should succeed."

The audience cheered furiously; the private secretary felt peace in his much troubled mind. Bright was almost the only man in England who hated Palmerston and was not afraid of him, or of the press or the pulpit, the clubs or the bench, that stood behind him. To an American he seemed more English than any of his critics. He had the British weakness of believing only in himself and his own conventions. An American saw much racial eccentricity, but little that was personal.
